utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. We have -- our next witness is Marko Prelec, who the Chamber has heard from before. And there are no protective measures. There is one part of his testimony that we may seek private session on, for reasons that I would explain in private session, not having to do with his personal security but other matters. But there is, other than that, no security measures. The testimony of the documents that are going to be used with this witness today go to two primary issues, not exclusively but primarily. One is existence of an international armed conflict, and of course, as you know by now, Your Honours, it's the Prosecution case that the Republic of Croatia and its forces were involved in this armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina between the Bosniaks and the Croats during 1993, and the early part of 1994, and that there was indeed an international armed conflict. The second principal topic will be the existence of widespread and systematic behaviour. That is also a prerequisite under the crimes against humanity charges in the indictment that the conduct be widespread and systematic, and Mr. Prelec will also be assisting in the presentation of some additional documents concerning that matter, the relevance of those particular documents being, again, to show that -- I think the Chamber will see, we submit, that the things that the Chamber has heard a great deal of evidence about now in Herzegovina were taking place simultaneously in other parts of Bosnia, primarily in central Bosnia, and that indeed the conduct was widespread and systematic. That's by way of introduction, Mr. President, and we will call Mr. Prelec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Did you furnish all those documents to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe we were in the process of doing that when we started -- when you came in. I'm going to start, Mr. President, with a bundle of documents that are going to be handed to you now and a table that has been listed as P893. I see Mr. Krsnik is on his feet. I'm not sure why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, and thank you, Your Honours. I will immediately explain why. We have received this list just now. We are not prepared -- with all the objections that we shall hear now from my learned friends, we thought that today we shall only have the presidential transcripts. I do not think it is right to receive, a minute before the hearing, a list, because we, like you, need to prepare to hear the list of documents to be tendered through Mr. Prelec a minute before we started, so that we, or at least I, had no time to check the documents which are on this list, go through them once again, in order to be on an equal footing with Mr. Prelec. That is one thing. And secondly, I believe that my learned friend has said that we shall not be talking about the substance, about the contents of the documents today, because if we do that, if we are discussing the substance of these transcripts, in that case, the Defence cannot conduct the cross-examination. The Defence is not ready for that. We explained it to you two days ago. We heard your ruling, and we comply with it. We can discuss documents as such, but the substance, the contents -- last night we leafed through these documents. We immediately realised two or three things, and we have to say something. I mean -- we mean the consistency, certain variances, certain differences. And again, this list -- I really cannot go through this list. I cannot go on looking for where these documents are. We received these documents only a minute ago, and I really -- Mr. President, Your Honours, please give us at least half an hour to read those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I want to know whether the documents listed in the Exhibit P893 have been furnished to the Defence counsel or you just provided the list this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The documents have been tendered. They've been in the 17 binders. The Defence has had the documents since early September, late August or early September. Your Honour, I'm not going to go into a long statement on this. Counsel's just wrong once again. If he would read his correspondence, and if he would just -- it's not true. We gave notice. I don't have the letter with me. I will once again, as I've done in the past, I will produce the correspondence to the Chamber indicating that we were going to call Mr. Prelec this week, including on this matter. I would be happy to provide that to the Chamber. Counsel has had these documents now for some months, for at least three months. The list is being provided simply as an aid, simply as an aid to assist everyone in knowing which documents we're talking about, and the documents themselves have been known to the Defence for over three months now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik, do you still want the floor? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I'm trying to say is that I cannot check if it is these 17 binders. That is, I cannot say whether I received them or not, because I have to check this. I have to go and see if I received them. By this, of course, I don't mean to say that my colleague -- my learned friend is not telling the truth. If he says we received them, then I believe we did receive them, but my learned friend knows he cannot give it to us a minute before we start. Even yesterday when we were talking, all he announced was the presidential transcripts. He cannot place us in such a position a minute before the witness is called in. That is not fair, my learned friend, regardless of what you think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, the problem is that we are under a very tight schedule, which means we have no time to lose for the court hours. What if we begin with this witness, first of all, on the presidential transcripts first? I believe that your co-counsel will check all those documents listed in Exhibit P893 to see whether they are in the 17 binders or not. Mr. Scott, call your witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We call Marko Prelec. If the usher could assist us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the interpreters also get a copy of the schedule if it is going to be used, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President -- I'm sorry. Mr. President, what I was about to say -- I apologise. I'm not sure what the witness -- what the hold-up is, but there are a total of eight of these binders. For the sake of less confusion and less volume for all of us, for Your Honours and for everyone in the courtroom, we are only going to be directing particular attention to a couple, again by example. I think one will be in volume 3 and one will be in volume 6. So those are the only ones we need to work with, I think. But there are a total of eight binders altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott, you have to know that your direct examination could touch upon the relevance of those documents to this very case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But you are not going into the substance of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I could just say, that is our full intent. When I say "substance," I'm not asking this witness to express any opinion or conclusions as to what the documents show or do not show, but as we've done before, I may ask the witness to assist the Chamber in terms of some of the information reflected on the face of the document which the Chamber might not be familiar with. But clearly, it is not my intention to ask this witness to express any opinion or conclusions drawn on the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, Judge Clark, Judge Diarra, I will not introduce this witness to you, because you've seen Mr. Prelec before. I would ask the Chamber, since we are taking these -- this category of documents first, if we could go to private session for a moment for a request, and then you can decide, Your Honour, whether you want to stay in private session or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, now just continuing on for a few minutes, in terms of the procedures again by which this material then was further reviewed, and without addressing the matters already touched upon, would it be fair to say then the material was reviewed, copies of selected material was requested, and that material would then -- the copies of that material would then be provided by the government of the Croatia to the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, in the same manner that you have -- you've informed this Chamber of before was the process by which the matter would be -- the material - excuse me - would be received into the Office of the Prosecutor, given various unique stampings and kept secured in the evidence vault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also tell the Chamber that in preparing and reviewing this material, just to confirm, if you will, the continuity of this material, have you seen transcripts in The Hague, in the Office of the Prosecutor, that are the same as transcripts that you saw when you were actually sitting in the offices of the President in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would direct your attention respectfully now, and counsel, to a table which has been prepared and admitted -- excuse me, tendered as Exhibit P892. It should -- I hope you have -- I'm told that they were -- originally there was a set in the first binder of the entire set, but I'm also told they have been made available today, I hope. Mr. President, do you have those on the bench? Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Prelec, is it correct that this then is -- what this document represents is essentially a schedule or listing with some summary material of selected -- approximately 36 selected transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of it me, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. I'm sorry. I thought it had already been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could we provide a copy to the witness, please? My apology. Mr. President, the schedule's probably rather, I think, self-explanatory, but let me just ask the witness a few questions by way of background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the exhibit number listed in the far left column, can you tell the Chamber briefly what information, what sort of information is listed or indicated in the second column from the left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the second column from the left, you have basically some sort of identification of what the transcript is. If it's a meeting of a formal group, a formal body, that's sometimes indicated. The date is always indicated and usually in a small group, all the participants and in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a larger group, just the first few or the more important participants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the -- is it correct that what is reflected in the -- what might be described as the middle three columns, that the binders that have been provided to the Chamber and to counsel include the full, what we call, B/C/S transcripts and the ERN number, the marking number? The record-keeping system of the Office of the Prosecutor is marked there, the number's given. There were then relevant excerpts translated and the numbers and identifications given for those items. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I believe the summary -- indication of summary will speak for itself. It may be that a better example of a listing of participants in a meeting -- well, we can perhaps -- one that we will get to, but if I could start -- if I could direct the Chamber's and counsel's attention to page 4, just simply as an example, for the PT3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this would be an example, again, listing at least some of the people who attended, what the meeting was about, in terms of who was there and some of the individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, are you familiar with the name Franjo Boras?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was one of the Bosnian Croat members of the Bosnian Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as usual, we have the same situation. A witness appears, we say that he is not going to testify to any facts, then they start slipping in facts, and then more facts are brought in. And the Prosecutor is doing this and then saying, "We are not going to do it," and then he does it anyway. And please, can we not allow this to go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I believe that the Prosecutor is just drawing our attention to that particular document. And Mr. Scott, would you please be very careful about those facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. And I've not asked -- what I've said consistently, and what I believe I've complied with, is I've not asked this witness to give -- express any opinion or conclusion. What I have asked him to do, and would continue to ask him to do, in some respects, is to give this Chamber some additional information as to some of the names and information reflected on the face of the document, simply to assist the Chamber but not to express any view on what the material shows or doesn't show. Now, what I would like in that regard, Mr. President, what I would like to do, and what I would propose to do -- and I'm, of course, as always, in the Chamber's hands. What I had intended to do was to look at two particular transcripts simply again to orient the Chamber to the material and indicate some names, get the assistance of this witness as to that, and be concluded with this part of the testimony. That's what I hoped to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, if I could ask Your Honours and would direct counsel's attention, then, to volume number 3, which is the one of the binders that was given to you this morning, and that counsel has had for sometime. And specifically I'm going to ask -- and the witness will need a set. I hope he has -- he will need a volume 3, and if -- if we didn't wind up with enough copies or binders in the courtroom, my apologies. If I could then direct Your Honours' attention to tab 11, which will be Exhibit PT -- and "PT" simply means -- for our purposes, at least, means, "Presidential Transcript" 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just looking at the first page, can you just tell the Chamber, is that -- I'm not suggesting they all look exactly alike, but is that the type of format that you saw -- that you've seen in looking at this transcript material that you've had access to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the Chamber will see, if you leaf down some number of pages - probably a couple of centimetres - you will, of course, find ultimately the B/C/S version, which is -- immediately follows the English transcript, if you go back. So it is there, and the entire B/C/S transcript is in the binder at that tab number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this regard, concerning a meeting -- a conversation between the President of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and the Minister of Defence on the 22nd of October, 1993, let me just get your assistance with a few names and background items. In the first page, about the -- below the middle of the page, there is a reference to a Mr. Susak, who the Chamber has heard about before, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we still see again that what Mr. Krsnik has objected to is being repeated, so I'm going to substitute for him. I think that we are now going into the substance. We are going -- we are not going about the contents or the text or even the names. We are going to the gist of what the Prosecutor is trying to argue. We can ask how this PT11 found itself here, how it was -- how did it reach the OTP, rather than have it read. In other words, we are reading and leading evidence from it, and I think that that is not what was agreed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me state -- I'm sorry, I defer to Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, there is confusion. And if I am responsible for that, I apologise. I did not indicate that I would not ask the witness some factual questions about the documents. What I've said consistently is that he would not express opinions or conclusions about the material or what the material shows. I'll give the Chamber an example, and then, again, as I say, I'm in the Chamber's hands. And I'm happy to proceed either way. We can certainly abbreviate this morning's proceedings if -- depending on what the Chamber wishes to do. Let me ask -- let me give an example. On the very first page is a reference to General Bobetko. I don't know -- and I certainly do not for a moment want to be considered insulting the Chamber's intelligence, but I don't know to what extent General Bobetko is known to you or who he was or his role or not. There are other names. And several pages down, there is a name of a Tole. There is that sort of information that this witness could provide the Chamber with some assistance on, and that's what I would propose to do. But again, of course, I'm in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, since there are some strong objections from Defence counsel, and as we said before this trial, that this witness is only going to lay some background of those documents, which means how they selected those documents and how they process with these documents in their hands. As for the substantive matters in this document, I don't think it's the subject of your direct examination at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I completely accept, of course, the Chamber's ruling, and that will certainly abbreviate these matters. So I will put those binders aside. Before leaving the presidential transcripts, Your Honour - I won't give it to you now - I'll just say this -- and the reason I'm not is it needs to be made sure that it's put in the proper spot. We did find yesterday, unfortunately, there was one portion of one transcript that the translation was missing. It's been done. I have these in hand. But at some point they will need to be inserted and -- so that the -- so it's complete. And my apology for that, but I do have them present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you inform us which document is this translation for?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This relates to -- it's part of transcript 28, PT28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, with that then, and with the Court's direction, which I'm grateful for, I would turn to the second set of documents, which is the material that we started talking about a few moments ago, and the list that is numbered 893.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, before you leave this subject, we wonder whether you could ask this witness to furnish this Chamber with a name list of who is who, which might be helpful in our deliberations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. I think we can certainly pursue that. We won't do that on the spot, obviously, but we can prepare that and produce it before the conclusion of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, if you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If he could be -- if he hasn't been, if the witness could please be shown a copy of Exhibit 893.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a copy of this document. Could it be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the translation -- benefit of the translation booths, I don't believe there will be any significant discussion of the table. Mr. President, this schedule goes to the other documents which I mentioned in my opening comments concerning the widespread and systematic nature of various things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, have you assisted in -- among the staff of the Office of the Prosecutor in the preparation of this material for presentation to the Chamber today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you also work extensively in the Kordic case that was tried before this institution in the past couple of years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you become, in the course of that work, quite familiar with the exhibit material, much of the exhibit material in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't be -- claim to be familiar with all of it. I think there were more than 2.000 exhibits, but yes, a very large number of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as part of the preparation of this document -- concerning these documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, again for the record, we do not have a separate compilation of all of these documents except for a small binder of sample documents which we prepared, but they are in the 17 binders of documents that have been tendered for some time, or - excuse me - to use the correct terminology, they were provided, and then various documents have been tendered or offered as the case has proceeded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of the preparation of this table, Witness, are you able to say that the Office of the Prosecutor, again as with the previous submissions that this Chamber has seen, when to look at the source -- to provide the source information regarding the various documents which is indicated in the column from the fourth -- the fourth column from the left of the page titled "Source"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if it says, for instance, the -- abbreviated here "Gov. BiH," that was information on request from the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the column immediately to the right of that column, can you again confirm to your knowledge based upon your involvement in this project and with the assistance of others that the -- all of the documents in fact listed in this document P893 are all exhibits that were admitted in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, my intention again here had been - and I will assume that the Chamber's guidance may well be the same - I have prepared a sub-bundle of approximately five or six documents which were provided -- distributed in the courtroom this morning, again with the idea that this witness, without expressing opinions, could provide some background information as to names of individuals, names of organisations. For instance, I'm simply -- I'm not even saying that people have to pull it out. But I'm saying as an example, the first document refers to something called the "Travnik Subregional Community." And I would ask, for instance, the witness to describe or give his information on what that entity was at that time. But again I'm in the Chamber's hands, and it may be that the Chamber's views and counsels' views, presumably, will be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Scott, if you have any information or questions that will help us to find our way through this document, we certainly welcome this kind of assistance from your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Mr. President. Well, I will try, and we'll see what we can do. And again, I'll accept the Chamber's guidance at any moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott can I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What we would be very interested in, I think, is hearing from this witness as to how, when he examined this huge volume of documents in the safe at the presidential palace, that he was able to select documents which he feels that this Trial Chamber should look at and how those documents are relevant to Mr. Martinovic and Mr. Naletilic. We haven't heard that yet. Because obviously there is a selection process which has been gone through, and we'd like to know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark. I think as to the first part, I can ask him to do that in terms of the further -- providing the Chamber with some additional information on the review and selection process. I fear that if we get into justifications of relevance, that we'll find ourselves back into drawing the objections of counsel, because that will involve him stating opinions and positions as to what relevance the documents are. I'm afraid -- I'd be more than happy to do that, and I hope that I can ultimately do that in our trial brief, in our final brief and my closing argument. But I fear counsel will give us the objections they've given us this morning already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go as far as we can, Witness, possibly. Can you give us a bit more background, assist the Chamber by indicating -- you've indicated that not only yourself but a number of representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor were involved in reviewing this material. And can you give the Chamber some idea the type of criteria that were used in selecting from among this substantial volume of material that you said was located in the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can -- yeah. The staff of the Office of the President had lists of all the material that they had in the safe broken down into various categories. There were -- for example, there was a large category of transcripts. Those were arranged by year. Then there were other transcripts that were one-on-one meetings between President Tudjman and one other person. Those were arranged separately and arranged by person. So I saw those indexes and just read through them and selected the ones not really with the issues of this case in mind at all but simply looking for material that might be of interest to the International Tribunal as a general matter. So I focused on the years of the war in Bosnia. I also focused to a degree on time periods of when important things had happened in Croatia. There were some areas that I didn't really feel competent to go Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. into at the time, so I tended to focus on my area of knowledge, which had to do mostly with Bosnia. So based on that, we made -- when I say "we," I made for myself, and other people working in the same way would make one for themselves, a preliminary selection of transcripts that we thought, based on date and participants, would be interesting and then read those. Sometimes it turned out that they had to do with, you know, discussions about the budget or things like this or some diplomatic event that had taken place. Sometimes it turned out that they were discussions that did actually bear on the war in Bosnia, and those then I made notes of, sort of short summaries, sometimes quite elaborate summaries, and requested copies. I understand there was then -- once all that material arrived here at the Office of the Prosecutor, a separate selection was made by other people, not by me, of what material to actually use in this case. So I can't really comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, I think with the parameters that have been given, that's about as far as I'm able to go. It may be that perhaps it could assist the Chamber. And I -- it would not be unusual in my system for counsel - of course my comments are not evidence - but for counsel to give some indication of the relevance. If the relevance of a proffered document is questioned, certainly counsel has to make some representations or statement as to relevance. If the Chamber would want that, I could provide some of that, but otherwise, I think that the presentation seems to be at an end for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we have some questions, we'll ask the witness on those particular questions. And if there is a necessity, we'll ask some submissions from both parties concerning those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examination? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Prelec. We have not yet had the privilege to meet, so allow me to introduce myself. I'm Kresimir Krsnik, lawyer and counsel for Mr. Mladen Naletilic. I will ask you some questions related to your today's examination-in-chief. And you understand Croatian, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand Croatian. I will answer in English for the benefit of the Chamber, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My first question will be: How did you get to the Office of the President? I don't mean -- of course I don't mean whether you used a bus or a car. I mean were you invited there or did you invite yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we request to go to private session for these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, if the direct examination is conducted in private session, as a rule, the cross-examination should be conducted in the private session. Let's go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me, but may I ask why? What is the reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have already stated my reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And Witness, I have to remind you that understanding Croatian is a strong point but sometimes it also has some disadvantage. For instance, in these proceedings, whatever you said will be translated into other languages, so please wait for a while after the counsel finished his question, because we have several times in the transcript we could not distinguish question and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, can you tell me in regard of the transcript that we received, are these all the transcripts or are there more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are more, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And they're in the possession of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them in the possession of the OTP, but there are many more that are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You set up the criteria as to which transcripts you were going to turn over to us and which not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Someone else. I was not involved in that, in that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You said that these transcripts were under lock and key in the office of the National Security Advisor. Can you be certain to me and to the Trial Chamber that no one before you had access to these transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't. In fact, I'm certain that they were accessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were these transcripts always there where you found them? Were they ever kept in another place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My colleague is reminding me to ask you: Who was the person who had set the criteria about which transcripts would come into our case and which would not, which would be selected for this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually don't know. I was simply given the list that you have as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, these were persons in the Office of the President who gave you the transcripts which they wanted to give you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think it's -- I have always assumed that it was the Office of the Prosecutor. I mean, probably Mr. Scott or his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm referring to the Office of the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we did change gears rather abruptly, Your Honour because at one point we were talking about which documents were selected for trial and then in the Office of the President. If that's in fact the clarification, then I have no objection. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Krsnik. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you be certain that the persons who appear on the transcript were aware of their being recorded, if they assume what is in the transcript does accurately reflect what was said? In other words, did these people know that they had been recorded? Did you talk with any of those? You said that there were 40 kilometres of tape, 40 kilometres of material.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there are a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't remember that testimony, Your Honour, anything about 40 kilometres. I think there was a reference to 10.000 or 15.000 documents. I don't remember anything about kilometres being mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It's also something new to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Between these 10.000 and 15.000 kilometres - sorry - documents - I'm sorry - did you ever encounter the name of client in any of that material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in at least one of the transcripts, and there may have been other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What year -- what year was that transcript from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The transcript I'm thinking of is from 1994. And I should point out that it was a reference to your client, but your client did not appear to be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to assist the Chamber, it is PT11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my mistake, it was PT28, Your Honour, and my apologies. PT28, dated the 2nd of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: 2nd September 1994. I believe this is outside of the scope of the indictment, but whatever, can you confirm, Mr. Prelec, that since President Tudjman's death, that is, from the death of Mr. Tudjman, to the time of the takeover of these transcripts, no one had access to these transcripts? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In -- except for you. That is, from the death of President Tudjman until the time when you took possession of the transcripts, do you know whether anyone had access to these transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who had the keys to the room where the transcripts were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was there, the National Security Advisor always had access. I believe they were kept somewhere in the inner offices of the President, but that's really all that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And do you know where these transcripts were kept in 1991, 1992, early 1992? Or to make things easier, was the President's office always at the location where it is now and where you received your transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was actually moved to that location at some point in the early 1990s, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In the 1990s, the Office of the President was where you went and found these transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the -- during the 1990s, my understanding is that -- well, there were a number of state offices that the late President Tudjman used. For the most part of the 1990s, it was at that location on Pantovcak. I believe, in the very early 1990s, he also used a facility in the old town of Zagreb, but I'm not sure of any of the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who guaranteed to you or who vouched for the authenticity of these transcripts? Who did guarantee it for you and how did they guarantee it for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if it was any one person. There was continuity in the Office of the President, in that the staff remained, to a degree, the same from the staff of President Tudjman to the staff of President Mesic. Some of the people I spoke with and dealt with on a daily basis had also worked for the late President Tudjman and actually had appeared in some of the transcripts. So I don't recall a specific moment when someone told me, "I hereby guarantee these," but the whole tenor of this working relationship I had implied that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you do not know that when Mr. Mesic took over the position, that in addition to some secretaries, everybody else on the staff was replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's not precisely true. The chief of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, you have to let the witness answer the question himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm not objecting to the content of the question -- of the answer, Your Honour, but I think this is a matter -- we are getting into a level of detail that I would ask to go into private session. These are staff -- some of these are senior staff members who may still be in the government. There is no reason other than embarrassment or political heyday for this information to be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course it will depend on the answer from this witness, but in the precautionary consideration, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was substantial, but I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell me how these transcripts were produced? Were these people present in the meetings and they took down the record as they were listening, or was it done subsequently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, only to remind the Chamber again this evidence is covered elsewhere. Because we're in public session, I won't say where, but this evidence is covered in detail in other evidence that's been put before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you suggest we go back to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if it would assist you, we can go to private session for a moment. I cannot address it in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go back to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know what -- how these transcripts were written, what was used to write them down? Was it on a typewriter? Was it on a computer, some other electronic equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them from -- at the latest, 1995, and perhaps earlier, were done on a word processor. And I know this because when I was examining them in the envelope -- each of the transcripts would be in a yellow manila envelope. For some of them, there was also a computer diskette that had one or more word processing files on it. The earlier ones appear to have been typed, in that they are in a common typewriter typeface. But beyond the appearance of the text, I have no further knowledge about what machine they were made on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So we can infer that the diskettes of these conversations also do not exist? In other words, we only have just bare transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said for some of them, yes, there is a diskette, but not -- not for the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We don't have the tapes. We don't have diskettes. We only have transcripts of which it is claimed that it is supposedly the same as the tape which we are missing and the diskette which we are missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking me to confirm that? I don't see the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. That is the question. You know that I can -- I can also offer you my comment and then ask you whether this was correct or not. We have just determined that there is -- there are no tapes, and you also said that the diskettes are also missing. So this is what I tried to have you confirm with my last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's correct. There are only a very few late tapes and, somewhat earlier, some diskettes. But beyond that, as far as I understand, there is only the paper copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, we are not here testifying about transcripts. You are also testifying about other evidence, including Zagreb archive. Tell me, how many intelligence services did these documents pass through before they reached you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with regard --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that without further foundation, Your Honour. Which documents are we talking about? Are we talking about something else? If we are talking about something else, I object that it's beyond the scope of direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you might clear up this question for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but of course I mean primarily these transcripts. I mean the documents which are enclosed, which we received today, a minute before the hearing started, and the Zagreb evidence. I mean everything. Mr. Prelec is here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me answer, I suppose, sequentially. The transcripts, as far as I know, were never handled by an intelligence agency of any kind. The -- I don't have anything to add to what I said in my earlier testimony about the material that's referred to as the Zagreb archive material. That was handled by at least two intelligence agencies of the Republic of Croatia, and some of it originated from intelligence agencies in Bosnia, Bosnian Croat entity. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. With regard to the last category, it originates from various sources. I understand that some of the material that comes from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina is prepared by an entity known as the Agency for Information and Documentation, which some would say is -- has an intelligence function. But I don't know the details of that institution. Or beyond my general institutional knowledge that some documents come from that agency, I couldn't tell you right now precisely which ones. I think that's a full answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prelec. Tell me, I haven't read all these transcripts, because I didn't have time to do that. I merely perused them. We were surprised that there is no logical sequence and that the numbers referring to the same subject - for instance, if it begins with a "J" and then there is a mark that says "3," then the fifth page is "LJ," and then one is missing, there is "5." We see that there is absolutely no logical sequence in these conversations. So could you explain it to us, how could that happen? Why is it that we do not have a sequence of numbers and it is the same meeting? The meeting is taking place on such-and-such a date, 2010 [as interpreted], the subject is President Clinton and President Tudjman are meeting. Now they have marked "J" and then "3" and then "5," and in other words "4" is missing, or it skips over and comes up with "LJ," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, it sounds like argument to me and not appropriate questions for the witness. It's pure speculation and argument by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, but counsel could ask about the numbering systems of those documents. You may answer the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We received the documents in a certain order, and that is the order in which they are given here now. When I read them, my impression was that the numerical sequence, which generally consisted of two numbers followed in this way: There would be a number "1/," then the first page would be "1," the second page "2," and so on up to maybe "6" or "7" or "8." Then it would go to number "2/1," and so on, and then to number "3/1," and so on. The initials would change also. I don't recall precisely how, whether they always matched the first number or not. That would be easy to check. My assumption at the time - and this again was confirmed later in further testimony - was that the initials corresponded to the person doing the transcribing, the first number to a tape and then the second number to the page number of that tape. I also believed that, because when the first number would switch, the text would overlap. So the very end -- so for example, the end of page 1/7 would be the same as the beginning of page 2/1; a sentence or part of a sentence would repeat. But beyond that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not trying at all. I did ask not to discuss the substance. But I'd like to quote a characteristic example, and that is transcript of a conversation, that is, an alleged conversation between Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Boras from Bosnia-Herzegovina with Mr. Manolic and Mr. Susak. It started in the absence of the president of the state. Now, I cannot say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have the citation of which transcript counsel is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Binder 1, transcript 3. The page is marked 00152, and it is 6/6LJ. Of course I'm not going to refer to the substance but a characteristic example that we came across. And I merely wanted to -- 6/6. 015, 015. Have you found it? And now all of a sudden it says, "President" - we don't know which president. Who -- it doesn't say anything -- that he entered the room, that everybody stood up. I think that is good manners. Then this says: "Will you tell me what you, ..." something. Then comma, then three points. "Coming back from Europe, did you achieve an agreement (yes)? And now what?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters - I apologise - but they do not know what page it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And before that, obviously this discussion went on for how many hours? Doesn't that sound strange to you? If everything is recorded in a room and the President enters a hall, I presume everybody stands up, everybody says -- everybody greets the President. After all, this is the Office of the President. Don't you expect some logic in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It doesn't seem peculiar to me at all. Often conversational speech, when written down, seems very strange because people break off in the middle of a sentence, begin another sentence, another thought. And this particular session is a fairly small, very high-level group without a lot of decorum and protocol. But no, I was -- I was not surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, tell me, please: Who compared the original with the translation? Do you know that? That is, the Croatian text with the translation; do you perhaps know who did the comparison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's a part of the International Tribunal that does this. I don't -- I'm not really acquainted with their inner workings, but it's the same for any other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It wasn't you. You speak both Croatian than English. You didn't go to see whether the original was identical with the translation, you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. On one or two occasions -- because I always read these initially in Croatian, and sometimes later I would look at them in English if I was planning to cite them in a paper or if I was working on an actual case. Sometimes something in English would strike me as odd, and I would then go back and check. And on one occasion, there was something that I personally would have put differently had I been translating, but I'm not a qualified translator. So the answer to your question really, though, is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm asking you it because in binder 3, what is in the Croatian original is missing in the English one. It is PT8, binder 3. A whole part is missing. I'll tell you. It says that it is the meeting between Franjo Tudjman, Alija Izetbegovic, Haris Silajdzic, Mate Boban. And in English, it says that Haris Silajdzic says something, but it doesn't exist in the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you point me to a page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: PT8. It starts with "RO." RO183. It is RO156 in the Croatian original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see what the problem is. They seem to be the same, for that page at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No. The page which is -- I merely told you which document. The problem is on RO156, and the English is RO183192. In the Croatian version, it's like this: The President says something, Izetbegovic says something, and then the President says something, and in the translation you have "President." And then Haris Silajdzic turns up, and then Mate Boban turns up, and then Hari Silajdzic turns up. And we don't have it in the Croatian at all; that is, in the English text there is something which is absolutely non-existent in the English version -- in the Croatian version - excuse me - and what is in Croatian is missing in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would guess - and if you'd like I can continue leafing through this - that this is a case where only parts of the entire transcript were translated into English, and therefore, the first page may have been translated and what appears as the English third page is actually the beginning of an excerpt that's later in the -- in the original. Leafing through this now, Haris Silajdzic does appear in the Croatian original. I'm looking for the precise line though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, all I needed to know is that not everything has been translated, because we who read the Croatian, especially my client, we of course assume that everything is translated. I later on went through the whole transcript, and such a page where Haris Silajdzic, and then Mate Boban, and then Haris Silajdzic take the floor, I could not find it in -- I couldn't find that sequence of speakers in any of -- on any of the pages, in any part of the transcript. I really went through it. You can see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, counsel and the Chamber may wish to refer to the table which has been distributed as Exhibit P892, which plainly indicates, and has been indicated all along, that English versions are excerpts. This institution has a huge problem with the volume of translated material that has to be done. The accommodation that was reached in the Kordic case was that the entire - and I suggest for this case - the entire B/C/S transcript has been provided, indeed the very language that counsel and his client speak. They have the entire transcript. They can read it. They can translate other parts if they choose. Selected parts were translated, were requested by the Prosecutor for translation for the purposes of saving translation, but the entire transcript is available to counsel. And there's no secret to that. It says it right on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please be so kind, my learned friend, and tell us in which table you're referring to so I can try once again? Thank you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you have to address to the Chamber, rather than to counsel directly. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the benefit of counsel, it is the table that was distributed to counsel some weeks ago. But it is P892. It's the table that was referred to -- has been referred to earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, do you know does Croatia have the presidential or the parliamentary system? I'm asking you if you know or if you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My -- do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness is an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- during the life of President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: At the time when you were given this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to relevance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for us to judge whether this question is relevant or not, but it doesn't hurt anybody if the witness answers this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would describe it as a mixed system, although predominantly parliamentary. It was mixed also before, but at that time, there was a much stronger accent on the powers of the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm asking you this to show the relevance, with the leave of the Court. Secondly, whose property are these transcripts that you found in the Office of the President? Whose property are these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... examined them. My understanding was that they were the property of the Office of the President. However, I do know that there has been a lot of debate within the Croatian government about this, and I don't know what the final determination, or for that matter if there has been a final determination about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. It is the property of the Croatian people and the decision whether something that belongs to the people and the state, as in your fatherland, the decision on that can be taken only by the parliament; isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, that's purely an assertion by counsel. I don't think we are here to be having civics lessons by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw. I withdraw. I withdraw my question. I withdraw it. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What I wanted to say: The decision that these transcripts could be given to you could be taken only by the parliament and nobody else. Such a decision could not be taken by the president of the state because he cannot dispose of those documents at his discretion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry, Witness. Same question -- same objection, Your Honour. It's purely an assertion by counsel. There is no evidence to suggest that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, Mr. Krsnik, you promised us that you would skip this question, but you come back through the back door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think he came back through the same door.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Clark, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What I'm trying to arrive at is this: Do you have a written authorisation of the Croatian government to use these documents in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there is such a thing, although I don't deal with -- it's a -- this is a very large organisation, and that's -- those issues are handled by others. But I do know that there was discussion about -- extensive discussion about whether they could be used or not, and there was a positive response. Permission was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you aware that the government cannot take such a decision without the parliament's authorisation? If you are aware of it, then you are. If you are not, then never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, same objection. Your Honour, I'm sure -- I'm quite confident counsel can put questions to this witness all afternoon and say, "If you're aware," "If you're aware," "If you're aware," and we will be here indeed until Monday. We hope to finish this witness today so we can finish our last witness, who is coming from Bosnia, on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. We won't, we won't, Your Honours. No, we won't be sitting until Monday. No. All I want to show this Chamber is whether these documents were obtained in a lawful way. I think it is relevant because the Defence puts it to the Chamber that these documents were not obtained in a lawful manner and that that is what we are talking about here. That is what we are challenging, that is, the authenticity of these documents. I didn't ask this question just like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think this is a valid point, but you have to pose it another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours. My colleague has just helped me to phrase this question as best I can, because I got confused again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So are you in possession of a document whereby the Republic of Croatia, that is, the supreme body, the parliament of the Republic of Croatia, approves the use of these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know of any decision by the Croatian parliament granting permission, but -- nor do I know that such a thing would be required. And I actually doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, then, do you know - since you evidently spent sometime in the Republic of Croatia, as far as I can see - do you know if all the documents from the Office of the President, whichever, have been proclaimed state secret and placed under seal for the next 30 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've heard something about that, but I'm not familiar with the details. I know there was -- I don't believe -- I think it was a government decision, but I don't -- I don't know the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. And by the decision of the parliament, the government has the executive power, passed such a decision because -- precisely because there was an abuse of this transcript -- of these transcripts in -- because they became public. But let's move on. Mr. Prelec, I'd like to move on to the second part of the documents. All I want to ask you is perhaps a question about a document Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. P128 -- well, as a matter of fact, I can do it. What are the sources? Where do these documents come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The source is noted in the source column. It's a variety of sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, do you have that document at your hand, Exhibit P128?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness has to be furnished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We didn't have this. Here. This 128 is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not believe it's one of the selected documents. I think it's one of the documents in the -- it is? Then I've been corrected. The Registry is correct. I think it's the second document in the small blue binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, it's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have it now in front of you, Mr. Prelec?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Where did you receive this document from, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's listed as Dzemal Merdan who was a general of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Beyond that, I don't know whether General Merdan brought it himself or whether he was simply the authenticating individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Fine. Now, since you have it in front of you, if you -- since you have this small binder, will you please look at P132. Just if you can answer me this: General Merdan is a general of which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was he a security officer, or is he a commander of the infantry, artillery, or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he was the deputy to General Hadzihasanovic of the corps in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean General Hadzihasanovic who is now in the detention unit of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if we can move to P132, did you -- have you found it? Can you please give us the origins of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know what -- what part of the government, but government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell me: What does this mean, this name up in the top, "Nezir Huseinspahic"? What does that name have to do with this document, this handwritten name? "Nezir Huseinspahic" is clearly a Bosniak name. And it's initialled on top of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And can you tell me whether you know that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina found all the original seals of the HVO in the northern camp and in other locations? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please tell me now -- now, in this list it's P139. I see that some -- some documents were tendered through a Witness D, but not 139. And through this Witness D, was that document tendered in the Kordic-Cerkez case? Do you know what this witness testified about? Of course if you cannot say, due to the closed -- but we have P139 and another number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what Witness D testified to, and I actually don't know who he is -- or she.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When you say "Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina" - and I see that the large majority of the documents come from them - what body are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I've already spoken that at least one body of the government which does furnish documentation from time to time is the Agency for Information and Documentation, known as the AID. But other parts of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina also respond to requests for assistance and binding orders from, respectively, the Prosecutor and the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And do you know about this Witness D? Do you know the documents that were tendered through this witness? This is P133 and 139.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the specific documents, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thank you very much. I have no further questions. Of course, I will provide written submissions about all the documents following the agreement from before. Thank you, Mr. Prelec, for your patience and your answers, and I hope we will meet in different circumstances the next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seric, any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I hope that we will be finished by 1.00, and I will hurry up, but not -- I will try to be slow enough to be able to be interpreted properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prelec, you said that according to your knowledge, these transcripts which have been provided to the -- this Trial Chamber and to the Defence were transcripts of some records, some audiotapes. Can you tell me, while you worked on gathering these transcripts and selecting them, have you been able to determine that these audiotapes had any kind of official form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: While working -- first of all, let me ask you this: Were you there as an investigator or some kind of advisor on the Prosecution team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my function is a researcher, a research officer. I suppose it was in a way an investigative function in this particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is why I'm asking this: In your attempt to find the original - that is, an audiotape - did you find anywhere that there was a permission given for recording?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should say I personally did not seek to locate audiotapes, since there had been discussion that preceded my actual arrival about how exactly to go about accessing this material, and it had transpired -- I knew -- I was told that the tapes had been re-recorded. It may have come up again in conversations with members of the staff, but I -- I did not go looking for tapes. The second part of your question, all I can say is that there are the references in some of the transcripts to people asking, "Is this being taped or not?" And in other testimony I've read, there was reference to visible microphones. So the possibility of taping would have been known to the participants. But whether any individual conversation was actually being taped, that would not necessarily be immediately obvious. And I don't know about permission or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: In your investigative work, were you able to determine whether this recording followed the legislation, the rules and regulations of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, my learned friend Mr. Scott asked you about the system of recording; however, I did not understand your answer. In your investigation about the authenticity, that is, the transfer of the record from one medium to another, did you -- were you able to determine where the microphones had been placed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. My knowledge of that simply comes from reading the transcripts in the Kordic proceeding where this was discussed. But I personally did not actually see that office, and I don't know whether the microphones are, in fact, still there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: In your work, were you able to learn who had set up these microphones? And I'm going to hurry up a little bit. And the follow-up question is: Who was supervising the -- or who was controlling the system, the equipment, the recording equipment? Were you able to find that out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My only information for that question would be the closed-session transcript in the Kordic trial to which reference has been made today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, you said that the transcripts were kept in a safe, or in a vault. I am not quite prepared for this -- for this question, but the Feral Tribune, a magazine - I could show it to you, I don't have it here - but this claims these transcripts have been shown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen both -- yes. I've seen material from transcripts in the Croatian press.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see that the persons who were mentioned in the transcripts that had been published in this media denied their participation in these conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't remember the exact contents of those media reports, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me when I analyse this whole method of recording, as a lawyer, with all these microphones, that we could not find any legal provisions that would not point to wiretapping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that's correct. It's clear that the participants, they're sitting in a room with visible microphones, and they're talking at times about -- in fact, at some times -- at least one occasion that I looked at recently, one of the ones that's submitted here or made available here, I think there's a request to -- to make a transcript. So at times, the participants felt they were speaking for the record, as it were. So the implication of your question, that this was covert and a type of illegal police behaviour, is, I think, completely mistaken. It's not like that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, did you talk about these transcripts with Mr. Miroslav Tudjman, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about these transcripts while you were in Zagreb and collected them, with Mr. Hrvoje Sarinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you talk with Mr. Ivic Pasalic, who was an advisor of Mr. Tudjman at that time and another participant of these conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to Mr. Josip Manolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: With Mr. Markica Rebic, who was the head of SIS, the Secret Service at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So how can you assert now that this was not wiretapping? And you have not laid any legal foundation for the recording of these tapes, and you have not talked to any of the participants, and the audiotapes are missing too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't comment on the legal -- the necessity or lack of necessity for a legal basis for a recording when it's done in public, when -- you know, it would be a different matter if it were a question of concealed bugs or wiretaps, although I'm aware that the Croatian media had a lot of discussion of that very different issue as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, I asked you a moment ago where the microphones were placed, and you did not know exactly. You just gave an assumption.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So now, please tell me: A moment ago we agreed - and I'm hurrying up because I'm trying to finish on time - you said that these transcripts were kept in a safe, and at the same time we agreed that they were also published in the media. Did you find out during your investigation that they disappeared from the safe and reached the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had to be some kind of leak. I thought it impolite to put that question to the members of the Office of the President, so I did not -- I did not ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that handling -- the handling of the transcripts which were in the safe was without control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, since at least some transcripts were distributed to some of the participants. There is the one that I referred to earlier, which one of the participants had and made available to the Office of the Prosecutor. So it -- not necessarily a handling without control.
