And I think leaks are familiar in many governments and do not indicate that the government in question is out of control or is handling its information in an insecure way. I think that implication can't really be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You have already answered in response to the questions of my colleagues that you were not in a possession of all the transcripts over a longer period -- that were produced over a longer period of time, that is, the transcripts of these recordings made in the Office of the Prosecutor, in other words, that there were other transcripts. Did you see that there were some transcripts that say the opposite of what the transcripts that have been provided here are saying? In political -- so what I'm -- my point is the politics change, and this is what we experienced in Croatia. Did you find transcripts that actually say things in a -- that shed a different light on events from the transcripts that we have here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't understand the question. I object to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And this question is kind of speculation, Mr. Seric. Maybe you could rephrase your question, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: It is a historic fact that the politics in the territory of former Yugoslavia - and this is a crucial issue to this case - the policies changed in such a way that it was -- that necessarily the contents of the conversations in the presidential palace changed. Did you find such transcripts too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, clearly, since I read transcripts from over at least a five-year period, the political positions taken by the -- the strategic positions taken by the participants changed over time from 1991, when the discussion was over the possible disintegration of Yugoslavia, through, later that year, the attack on Croatia and how to respond, and so on over time, initial relation with the government of Bosnia in 1992 that I would describe as somewhat tense but not hostile, through the period of open conflict in 1993 and so on. So, yes, there is -- there are different positions taken. But I can't really answer your initial question about other transcripts saying something different without a more -- without a specific point that -- that I would respond to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I regret, Mr. Prelec, that I don't have these other transcripts with me. I only have the ones that have been published in the media, that they say something different, because I address -- I went to both the Feral Tribune and to the president's office without success. So it would appear that I'm talking without a proper foundation. But I have read these transcripts that speak differently, and we are now unable to put it in front of you. So this is why I'm saying we would like to have been able to have all these transcripts before this Tribunal. Wouldn't you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I could say is that if there were a particular factual issue or statement that's made in one of the transcripts presented here, I could answer whether there is any contrary assertion, different assertion, made in other transcripts that I'm aware of, which is not all of the transcripts. I haven't read all of them. But I guess the -- I don't know what to say to the question of whether you would like to have all the transcripts before this Tribunal. I -- I just don't know what to say to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, only about two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, during the time, the extensive time you were dealing with these officials, did any information come to your attention of any sort that suggested that the transcripts were not accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During these -- the period that you were dealing with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. officials of the Croatian government, was there anything said or done that suggested these were considered to be anything other than accurate records of the meetings and conversations recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. And the whole atmosphere of these meetings was such that everyone assumed we were talking about accurate material. I recall one of the persons mentioned earlier in today's testimony looking through some of these indexes and saying, "Well, I'm in here." And it would simply be very strange to me if, having then noticed that, if he had actually suspected that there was something inaccurate, not then to have said so. So it's maybe too elaborate an answer to your question but, no, there was never any implication that these were anything other than genuine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from Judges? Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, as a political historian - and I think you told us on the last occasion that you had prepared your doctorate on the basis of early twentieth century rise of nationalism in Yugoslavia - can I take it that you would have had access to a fair number of state archives for that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And I take it that before you arrived at the position of preparing for your doctorate, that you would have had access to research by other people of state archives from different periods and different countries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a very large quantity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is there anything unusual, therefore, in the fact that records were kept, minutes kept, of meetings between heads of government and invited guests or participants in the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There is -- there are the famous examples from my own country's history of the Nixon and Johnson tapes. But I think it's actually quite -- it's not an uncommon practice at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Say in the days before electronic recording, it would be quite normal for a minute, a detailed record, in shorthand to be kept of presidential meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have to be careful in answering that because I have actually never worked with presidential level records from the age prior to that of electronic recording. So I don't know. But I would assume that it would not be unusual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prelec, on the basis -- on the basis of which conversation? I asked you, and Judge Clark also asked you, and what you gave in response. How can you guarantee that the authenticity when there is no tape, there is no diskette? You did not ask -- conduct conversations with any of the participants. Who was -- you don't have -- Nixon and Johnson are tapes, and we all know about it. All we have is just a bare transcript. So on the basis of what can you say that this was an original? What is the basis of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is -- I may be repeating myself, but I have spoken, as I alluded to, to two members of the Office of the President who appear in these transcripts and a third person who also appears in these transcripts. And I also recall one of the names that your colleague brought up, who I believe - my memory may fail me - I'm referring to Mr. Sarinic - commented that yes, these were, in fact, accurate representations but that -- I'm just really -- it's a faint memory of an article I read a long time ago. But my personal testimony would be of these three individuals. And so I think yes, I can make that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prelec. I understand your position here, but it is one transcript. What about all those others? There are millions of names, millions of people featured here. And I'm asking you: How can you say that that is an original if you had no -- nothing else to show to this Tribunal? You come here to this highest judicial instance, and you claim that. And I'm asking you: If you talked with those three -- if you say three persons, then what about 10.000 others that you didn't talk to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is repeat of cross-examination. This does not arise out of Judge Clark's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. I withdraw my questions. I withdraw my questions. And I see that the time is up. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one question, Mr. President, and this arises from Judge Clark's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are an historian and have experience in that. Did you study French history during de Gaulle when they also had sort of a semi-presidential system, as in Croatia? Did you find in that part presidential transcripts or anywhere else, for that matter, in your scientific research, your work in some other country? Do you have any such example anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not from France, because I've not studied France, but I did some work in the American National Archives on the Nixon administration's policy towards Yugoslavia, and there was some material there concerning a meeting between the President and President Tito and various other officials, including Henry Kissinger. I don't recall off the top of my head whether it was a transcript. I think it may have been more of an extensive summary note. But yes, it was written. There was no reference to a tape. So that would be one example. But for France, I couldn't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness, for helping us by giving your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, I understand that the Prosecutor is going to tender all those documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As to the presidential transcripts, we tender all those which are listed on P892. I certainly won't take the time to read them all off into the record, but starting with PT/ -- excuse me -- -1, going to PT/36, but again all listed in P-829. We also tender all of those documents on P893, and again starting with P113.1 and continuing to P743.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the information. I understand that the Defence counsel will object to the admission of that evidence. You have 30 days to submit your objections in written form. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please, could you give us longer notice? Because it's more than 4.000 documents, really. Could we have more time for it? And we're starting on the 7th of January. And what about Christmas? And we are finally going home. We could have left today rather than on Monday, but well -- I mean, I asked our learned friends to make us a small Christmas gift and give us Monday so as not to have to stay here over the weekend. No. I'm just joking, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... schedule, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we are -- we shall be away for Christmas holidays. We shall have to study this. And we need some rest, like everybody else. We need at least a ten-day holiday. After all, we're entitled to some rest. And I do not think that my learned friends will object to that. Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you promised me yesterday that you'll spend all your Christmas reading all those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did. I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did. I did. I admit I did, but you know how busy I'll be. I'll have to make everybody else have to work. My colleague, he has said, "See what you've promised now? I'll have to do that." No. Sorry. Perhaps this is slightly facetious, but yes, of course, I'll be working, and I'll be back in Bosnia and so on and so forth. But could we have a bit more time for all that? This is our request. If the Prosecution doesn't object, I don't think that anything terrible will happen if it's 45 instead of 30 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me hear the response from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, again it's not 4.000 documents. In fact, it's quite a small number of documents. There's 36 transcripts and probably another 60 or so documents. Now, I don't think it's necessary for counsel to do an analysis of every document. Presumably the objections are going to be the same things that were mentioned today: lack of adequate foundation, et cetera. In fact, we've probably all heard it today, frankly, and I supposed that that will be transferred into paper form. So I don't think it's burdensome to do that in roughly 30 days or so. Maybe 35 days is a compromise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, everybody is entitled to a holiday after a long period of work, and we'll give you 40 days to respond to these documents on the condition that if the Prosecutor would like to make a reply to all those objections, then we should give them an opportunity to do that. Could I get your agreement on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will adjourn until 9.30 next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
